On Blame, Triggers, and What Really Causes Things

The Trigger Is Not the Cause

Why the person closest to a disaster is often not the real reason it happened.

Domain — Cause and Blame
Reading — 12 Minutes
Register — Diagnostic
Central Thesis

Being close to something bad does not mean you caused all of it. A person can start a chain of events without being the reason it turned out the way it did.

I. A Story You Already Know

A company loses its biggest client. By the next day, everyone in the office has a reason why: the account manager sent one email at the wrong time.

A family stops talking after a wedding. Within a week, everyone agrees on who ruined it: the cousin who said one thing during the toast.

You have probably seen this happen. Something goes wrong. Right away, people find one person to blame. One person, one action. That becomes the whole reason. It happened, they say, because of that one person.

There is an old story that shows this very clearly. In an ancient story called the Ramayana, a palace servant named Manthara says a few sentences to a queen. Those sentences change everything. A prince is sent away from his home for fourteen years. A king dies of sadness soon after. For thousands of years, people have told this story as if one servant, in one short talk, caused it all.

You may feel that same pull. It is a simple answer. It gives you someone to blame. It ends the story quickly.

II. The Story Most People Believe

The belief behind this reaction is simple: whoever is closest to the moment something breaks is the reason it broke.

This makes sense. When you look for the cause of something bad, you look for the last thing that happened before it. That is easy to see. Everything before it — years of small choices, old debts, quiet anger — is much harder to see. So the mind picks the thing it can see, and calls that the cause.

In Manthara's story, this belief holds up well. She really did go to the queen. She really did know which fear to press on. She chose her words on purpose, to get one result, and she got it. She was not just someone standing nearby by chance.

The belief feels true because the person we can see really did act, on purpose, to get a result. That is why it is so easy to stop the story there and look no further.

III. Where the Story Breaks

But one question does not go away: could Manthara have caused any of this alone, if nothing else had already been in place?

Years earlier, the king had made two promises to the queen. He had promised to give her anything she asked for, twice, at any time she chose. He made that promise long before Manthara ever spoke. The queen already had the power to demand the exile and the throne. Manthara did not give her that power. She only pointed at it.

There is more behind the scene, too. The king already carried an old, private pain — something he had done years before, in fear, that had already shaped him into a man who would keep his word no matter the cost. That pattern did not start with Manthara either.

And after her words were spoken, other people still had to choose what to do. The queen chose to make the demand. The king chose to keep his promise instead of breaking it. The prince chose to accept the exile instead of fighting for the throne that was his. Each of these was a separate choice, made by someone who was not Manthara. Each one shaped what happened just as much as her words did.

If Manthara's short talk were the whole cause, none of this earlier history should matter. But it clearly does. Something was already standing there before she ever spoke. She did not build the house. She lit a match near it.

IV. What Was Really Happening

Here is what was really going on, once you break the story into its parts.

There are three parts. Once you know them, they are easy to spot. First, the trigger — the thing you can see, right before the bad thing happens. Here, that is Manthara's talk with the queen. Second, everything that was already there — all the things already in place before the trigger, that let the trigger work at all. The old promise. The old pain. Years of a king bound tightly by his own word. Third, the choices that came after — what other people did once the trigger happened. Each choice could have gone a different way, and each one shaped the final result just as much as the trigger did.

A Closer Look — The Two Promises

The queen's power to demand exile did not come from Manthara's words. It came from a promise the king made years earlier, for a completely different reason. That promise sat quietly for years, doing nothing, until someone finally asked for it. Manthara's part was to point the queen toward something she could already ask for. She did not create that power. She used a fear that was already sitting in the queen's heart, long before Manthara ever arrived.

A trigger only works because everything around it is already dry enough to catch fire. The same words, said to a king who had made no such promise, would have done nothing. We tend to miss this, because the things already in place are slow and hard to see, spread out over years. A trigger is fast and easy to see — it happens in one moment. So the trigger gets remembered as the whole story, and everything that came before it quietly disappears.

This is why blame so often lands on whoever spoke last, or acted last, and stops there. Not because that part is wrong — the trigger is real, and it matters. But because it is usually the only part anyone could actually see.

V. A Clearer Way to See It

There is a clearer way to think about this. It splits one question into two: who started this, and who is responsible for everything that happened after?

Manthara started something. That is not in question, and nothing here changes that. She spoke on purpose. She knew exactly what fear she was using. What she did was wrong. Holding this clearly does not go against anything that comes next.

The real question is whether she is the whole reason for everything that followed. She is not. A king's old promise, a pain he carried alone, and the separate choices of at least three other people all had to stay in place for her words to end in exile and death. Take away any one of those, and the outcome likely changes — even with her words left exactly the same.

The one who lit the match did not build the house from dry wood. Both matter. Neither one excuses the other.

So here is the clearer way to see it: a person can start a chain of events without being the whole cause of where that chain ends. Being close to the outcome is not the same as being fully responsible for it. This does not make the person who started it innocent. It just makes the story complete.

VI. What This Changes

Once you see the difference between a trigger and a full cause, this way of thinking helps in other parts of life too.

Yourself

When something painful has happened to you, and one person's action feels closest to it, ask what else was already in place before they acted. This does not erase what they did. It gives you a fuller, truer picture of your own story — one that does not turn everything into one villain and nothing else.

Relationships

In a fight, whoever says the cruel thing first usually gets blamed for the whole fight. But a fight rarely starts from nothing. Asking what was already there — old hurt, an unmet need, a tiring week — does not excuse the cruel words. It explains why they hit so hard, and what would need to change so the same thing does not happen again.

Right and Wrong

Two things can be true about a person at the same time: they did something wrong, and they were not the only reason for what happened. Choosing to see only one of these is usually the easier path — full blame, or full excuse. Seeing both at once is harder. It is also more honest.

Groups and Families

When a company or a family finds the person who set off a problem, blames them, and stops there, the real weak spot — everything that was already in place before the trigger — never gets fixed. The same conditions stay, ready to cause the same kind of problem again, with a different person lighting the match next time.

VII. Questions to Sit With

Not to answer quickly. Just to let in.

  • Think of something painful that you still blame on one person. What was already in place before they acted?
  • Where in your own life have you lit the match, when the real weight belongs to something you did not build?
  • Is there someone you have quietly let off the hook because you decided they weren't really the cause — when they actually did do something wrong?
  • What would change if you held someone responsible for their action, without asking them to carry the whole outcome alone?

The story of Manthara has lasted for thousands of years because it is satisfying in a simple way — one person, one moment, one clear reason for everything that came after. But a promise made years earlier, a pain carried in silence, and three separate choices made by three separate people were already standing there before she ever spoke. She lit what was already dry. That does not make her innocent. It makes the story, as most people tell it, incomplete.

Closing Assets
Most Important Insight
A trigger and a full cause are not the same thing. The person closest to an outcome is often the easiest to see, and the least complete explanation for it.
Most Memorable Quote
"The one who lit the match did not build the house from dry wood."
Strongest Diagnostic Question
If you removed this person's action, would everything already in place still have led to a similar outcome, sooner or later, some other way?
Strongest Reflection Question
What would change if you held someone responsible for their action, without asking them to carry the whole outcome alone?
One-Sentence Summary
Being closest to something bad does not mean you caused all of it — a person can start a chain of events without being the only reason for how it ends.
